A Tearful Review from an 86-Year-Old Gamer: After Playing Alien Swarm, My Body, Mind, and Every Organ Are Different
Intro

Hello, young gamers. I am 86 years old. On the day my pension came in, my grandson added some money to my Steam account and said, “Grandpa, play this. It’ll prevent dementia.” Well, the dementia is definitely gone now—because I don’t have a brain left to get dementia. The aliens ate it.

1. Physical Changes
1. Hands

I used to shake. Parkinson’s-level shaking. I could pick up a peanut with chopsticks and my hand would blur like a hummingbird. After Alien Swarm, my hands don’t shake anymore. Now I can headshot six aliens in a row while calmly telling my team, “Bugs on the left, throw a fire grenade.”

But there’s a problem: now when I pick up a peanut with chopsticks, I instinctively hit R to reload. Yesterday at dinner I “reloaded” a bowl of rice onto the floor.

2. Eyes

Eighty-six years of life taught me to accept my limits. Alien Swarm taught me that people who accept their limits get eaten by bugs. Now I can spot a medkit versus an ammo box on a screen full of bugs. My eyesight went from “can’t read the TV guide” to sniper-level.

The cost: when I see a cockroach in real life, my first thought is, “How much HP does it have? Headshot or body shot?”

3. Heart

Doctors used to say I had an irregular heartbeat and told me not to get too excited. Now my heart has evolved into an Alien Queen model—four layers of armor and a metronome. Every time a bug swarm shows up, my heart rate goes from 70 to 180 and stops exactly at “one beat away from death.”

The doctor calls it “stress-induced tachycardia.” I call it “professional gamer physiology.”

4. Bladder

This one needs its own section.

At 86, my bladder used to run on a once-an-hour schedule. After Alien Swarm, my bladder learned to hold it until a teammate says, “We’re safe, take a break.” Yesterday I played a 47-minute match and held it until the whole team extracted. When I finally stood up, my legs were numb and I dropped to my knees.

My grandson said, “Grandpa, are you licking your teammates’ boots?”

I said, “Nonsense. I’m paying my respects to the aliens.”

5. Spine

I used to be hunched over, walking like a question mark. Now I have to sit up straight for Alien Swarm—because I need to scan the screen for bugs. After one week, my back doesn’t ache, my lower back doesn’t hurt, and I walk with a breeze.

My neighbor asked if I was taking some miracle supplement. I said, “No. I just get chased by aliens. Run enough and you straighten out.”

6. Ears

At 86, I used to need a hearing aid to hear my grandson call me for dinner. Now my ears have evolved into a sonar system—I can tell exactly which vent an alien is crawling out of, and I can even hear a teammate reload and shout “Cover me!” before they do.

Yesterday I heard the neighbor’s cat meow, and my first reaction was: “We’ve got a lurker in Sector B2. Watch out!”

2. Mental and Emotional Changes
1. My Understanding of Death

At 86, you worry a bit about death. After Alien Swarm, death became a button: “Press space to respawn. Keep going.”

Now when my grandson asks if I’m afraid of dying, I say, “Why? It’s just a cooldown.”

2. My Understanding of Friendship

I used to think friends were people you play chess with, drink tea with, and chat with. Now I think friends are people who run over with a chainsaw when an alien pins you down—and then accidentally saw you in half too.

My grandson asked, “Grandpa, why don’t you play chess with Old Zhang anymore?”

I said, “Zhang is useless. He can’t even use a healing gun. We’re not on the same level.”

3. My Attitude Toward Life

Eighty-six years of life experience told me: be steady, be careful. Alien Swarm taught me: “Steady is useless. Push forward and kill everything.”

Yesterday my grandson saw me sitting at the computer with coffee and asked what I was doing. I said, “Waiting for the next bug wave.”

He said, “Grandpa, you’ve changed.”

I said, “Yep. I used to wait to meet God. Now I wait to kill bugs.”

3. Official Complaints from My Organs
Brain: “Owner, I’m for thinking about life, not calculating alien spawn timers.”

Stomach: “Owner, I’m for digesting food, not cramping every time a bug wave comes.”

Lungs: “Owner, I’m for breathing, not holding my breath while sniping aliens.”

Knees: “Owner, I’m for walking, not sitting in a chair for an hour and then refusing to stand up.”

Tongue: “Owner, I’m for tasting food, not getting bitten bloody while gaming.”

Heart: “Everyone shut up. I’m the one complaining here. I’m beating like this and you don’t hear me?”

4. Final Verdict
After one week of Alien Swarm, my body has gone from an 86-year-old man to an 86-year-old man with an irregular heartbeat, a bladder that makes his legs numb, hands that don’t shake but will reload anything, ears that think every cat is an alien, a mouth that yells “bugs on the left” at the screen, and a grandson who says, “Grandpa, you’ve lost your mind”—but I still think I’m cool.

Score: 10/10

Reason: I’m 86 and I can still fight aliens. What’s your excuse?

P.S. Old Zhang, if you see this, don’t be mad. Tomorrow we’ll team up and I’ll teach you how to use the healing gun. Stop shooting aliens with it. It’s for healing, not shooting.

P.P.S. Grandson, when next month’s pension comes in, buy me the Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop DLC. Grandpa isn’t too old to spend money on games.

P.P.P.S. Aliens, listen up. I’m 86. My hands don’t shake. My eyes don’t blur. My bladder can hold it for 47 minutes. Are you sure you want to fight me?

—Love,
Grandpa Li, 86 years old, still waiting for the bug wave in Sector B2.
